ex_ante_forecast.evidence: The study shows that SVM is the leading model in “luxury and upscale” hotel room price forecasting, followed by RBF and then ARIMA (p. 1633)

F2_naive_or_seasonal_naive_benchmark.evidence: These methods include linear models (simple moving average and ARIMA) and non-linear models (radial basis function (RBF) and the support vector machine (SVM) (p. 1624)

F3_scale_free_or_relative_measure.evidence: MAPE 0.0345 0.0521 0.0289 0.0222 (Table 4. Performance for all cities, Dubai row, p. 1632)

F4_statistical_test_of_accuracy.evidence: When comparing the forecasting accuracy of different models and for the eight different cities, it was found that SVM and RBF performed better than ARIMA (p. 1633)

F5_no_information_leakage.evidence: The inclusion of external economic factors could also be one reason why these models outperformed the conventional models. (p. 1633)

F6_horizon_specified.evidence: The data split is done to test the models’ performance in predicting unknown observations (p. 1627)

F7_prediction_intervals.evidence: The following table (Table 4) represents the result of the models’ performance measures for each city as a measure of forecasting accuracy. (p. 1631)

notes: Table 4 does not label whether errors are test or training; Figure 3 is titled 'Out of Sample Data'. Error magnitudes appear to be on a transformed (first-differenced) scale; RMSE printed as percentages >100% and some MSE>RMSE^2 inconsistencies (e.g., Beirut ARIMA MAD 0.7123, RBF MSE 0.342) suggest reporting errors. Annual macro indicators (GDP growth, inflation, oil price, WEF indices) held constant within each year and arrivals = annual/365, so test-period values of annual indicators would not be known at the forecast origin; exact ML input set not listed. Only MAPE (all cities) plus selected Dubai SVM values extracted; MAD/MSE/RMSE for all cities are in Table 4. Hypotheses H1/H2 claims (moderation) are not formally tested.

setting: Saudi Arabia, city-level tourist arrivals (Vision 2030); external validation on Thailand domestic tourism data
data_source: Collected in collaboration with the Saudi Arabia Council’s Tourist Authority; data availability cites Saudi Ministry of Tourism domestic tourism dashboard (mt.gov.sa); external: Thailand Domestic Tourism Statistics Dataset

holdout.detail: Scenario A: 80/20 random split mixing years (374/94); Scenario B: train 2021-2022, test 2023 (312/156); Scenario C: 10-fold TimeSeriesSplit; Scenario D: SMOGN 1243/311
holdout.evidence: Dataset 2 used data from 2021 to 2022 for training and 2023 for testing, representing a realistic year-ahead forecasting scenario (p. 5)

F.horizon: year-ahead (2023 test, Scenario B); long-horizon projections 2024-2034

ex_ante_forecast.detail: 2024-2034 projections; VotingR2 from roughly 35 million (2024) to nearly 88 million (2034)
ex_ante_forecast.evidence: forecasting an increase from roughly 35 million tourists in 2024 to nearly 88 million by 2034. (p. 14)

F1_holdout_reported.evidence: models are trained exclusively on historical data (2021–2022) and tested on the unseen year 2023 using Dataset 2 (p. 11)

F2_naive_or_seasonal_naive_benchmark.evidence: the traditional time series models, ARIMAX and Prophet (p. 9)

F3_scale_free_or_relative_measure.evidence: Key metrics such as MAE, MSE, R² scores, precision, and F1-scores are employed to assess predictive accuracy and robustness. (p. 9)

F4_statistical_test_of_accuracy.evidence: the VotingR2 ensemble maintained the best overall performance (MAE = 0.0339, R2 = 0.8736), as shown in Table 6. (p. 12)

F5_no_information_leakage.evidence: Total Expenditure (Cost): Total spending associated with the visit. (p. 5)

F6_horizon_specified.evidence: Scenario B evaluates the model’s ability to perform forward-looking, year-ahead forecasting (p. 11)

F7_prediction_intervals.evidence: The final results were reported as the mean and standard deviation across all folds (p. 15)

notes: Contemporaneous 'Cost' (total visitor expenditure, same month/city) is the dominant predictor and its actual test-period values are used for test predictions; for 2024-2034 Cost was itself forecast with Prophet. Errors are on max-normalised scale. Scenario A uses random mixed-year split (temporal leakage). Text is internally inconsistent on long-horizon method ('controlled linear increments (0.05/year)' and Fig. 7/8 captions vs Prophet-driven feature extrapolation). R2 0.8735 in abstract vs 0.873587 in Table 6. Dataset only 3 years; ARIMAX/Prophet evaluated only under random split (Table 4). Publication year 2026 (Sci Rep 16:2556).

F2_naive_or_seasonal_naive_benchmark.evidence: By leveraging the SARIMA and SARIMAX models, this study compares the predictive power of intrinsic seasonal patterns against external economic and behavioral factors. (p. 5)

F3_scale_free_or_relative_measure.evidence: The performance metrics included are as follows: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE); Mean Absolute Error (MAE); Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE); Theil’s U statistic. (p. 7)

F5_no_information_leakage.evidence: the parameters of the SARIMA and SARIMAX models are identified by selecting the configurations that yield the lowest error terms on the Test data (p. 7)

notes: Setting is Turkey (check MENA eligibility). Model orders selected on Test-set error (test set not a true hold-out). Model assumption checks not reported ('not included in detail'). Text typo '2025 to 203' for the ex-ante horizon. Test period includes post-COVID recovery; training includes 2020 shock without intervention dummies (n/r). Regional SARIMA/SARIMAX error values not reported numerically. Tourist arrivals data source not stated.
